questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
- Tests practical hardening in a real repo
- Exercises policy-as-code and CI integration

## Key Concepts
- Kyverno policy, Kubernetes securityContext, multi-resource kinds, CI gates

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-container-hardening
spec:
  validationFailureAction: enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-container-security
    match:
      resources:
        kinds: ["Deployment","StatefulSet","DaemonSet"]
    validate:
      message: "Containers must have readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, privileged: false; pod runAsNonRoot: true"
      pattern:
        spec:
          template:
            spec:
              containers:
              - name: "*"
                securityContext:
                  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
                  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
                  privileged: false
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (privileged: true)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: alpine
        securityContext:
          privileged: true
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (proper hardening)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hardened
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: alpine
        securityContext:
          readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
          allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
          privileged: false
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test the policy coverage for Jobs, CronJobs, or custom resources?
- How would you version and migrate policies across repo branches and environments?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests ability to express policy-as-code for security/compliance in multi-cloud clusters, combining network isolation, identity controls, and outbound security.

## Key Concepts
- Gatekeeper/OPA ConstraintTemplate
- NetworkPolicy as runtime guard
- Pod securityContext and automountServiceAccountToken control
- mTLS and central CA validation for outbound traffic
- CI verification using kubectl, gatekeeper audits

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8snetworkidentity
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sNetworkIdentityConstraint
  targets:
  - target: Kubernetes
    rego: |
      package k8snetworkidentity
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        input.review.kind == "Deployment"
        not has_ns_deny_ingress(input)
        msg := "Deployment namespace must have a deny-ingress NetworkPolicy and allow only whitelisted sources."
      }
```

```yaml
# Failing manifest (no deny ingress and automount enabled)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-fail
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: example-fail
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: example-fail
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

```yaml
# Passing manifest (deny ingress, trusted SA, automount disabled)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: app-sa
  namespace: dev
  annotations:
    trusted.example.io: "true"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: example-pass
  namespace: dev
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: example-pass
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: example-pass
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: app-sa
      automountServiceAccountToken: false
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:alpine
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
```

```yaml
# Minimal NetworkPolicy (deny ingress by default, allow from trusted namespace)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: deny-ingress
  namespace: dev
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          env: trusted
```

## CI Verification Steps
- Gatekeeper audit run in CI to ensure constraints are evaluated.
- kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f failing.yaml should trigger policy violations.
- kubectl apply -f passing.yaml should succeed and Gatekeeper should record no violations.
- Validate that namespaces have the required NetworkPolicy objects and that deployments use trusted SAs with automountServiceAccountToken disabled.

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to design a scalable, automated policy gate across multi-cloud clusters using Gatekeeper/OPA, Cosign attestations, and runtime security constraints.

## Key Concepts

- Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate and Constraint
- Cosign attestation and image provenance
- Registry allowlist and image provenance checks
- Pod security: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem, drop capabilities
- CI integration and gatekeeper audit verification

## Code Example

```yaml
# ConstraintTemplate (Gatekeeper) minimal sketch
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8ssecuredcontainers
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sSecuredContainers
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8ssecuredcontainers
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not signed(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Container image %v must be cosign-signed", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not allowed_registry(container.image)
          msg := sprintf("Registry %v not in allowlist", [container.image])
        }
        
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
          not container.securityContext.runAsNonRoot
          msg := "Container must run as non-root"
        }
```

## What to Look For

- Demonstrates understanding of OPA/Gatekeeper policy structure
- Shows proper cosign attestation validation approach
- Includes comprehensive runtime security constraints
- Outlines practical CI/CD integration strategy

## Why This Is Asked

Tests ability to implement a basic software supply chain gate: SBOM generation and vulnerability scanning integrated into CI, with clear pass/fail criteria.

## Key Concepts

- SBOM generation with Syft
- Vulnerability scanning with Trivy
- GitHub Actions workflow basics
- Exit-code driven gates and report interpretation

## Code Example

```yaml
name: SBOM and vulnerability gate
on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t service:latest .
      - name: Generate SBOM
        uses: anchore/syft-action@v0
        with:
          image: service:latest
      - name: Trivy scan
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@v0
        with:
          image: service:latest
          severity: HIGH,CRITICAL
          format: table
          exit-code: 1
```

```dockerfile
# Failing Dockerfile (vulnerable)
FROM debian:stretch-slim
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/contract-ci.yml
name: Contract CI
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  validate:
```
